item.title: Stanford's century-long AI study admits it's already out of date
item.description: Twelve years into Stanford's 100-year study of artificial intelligence, the project's third report raises more questions than it answers. The 2026 AI100 Study Panel report acknowledges its limitations in its twelfth takeaway: "This report will be out of date by the time you read it." But it's nonetheless a worthwhile exercise for those who haven't been paying close attention to the development of machine learning over the past few years and for policymakers who may benefit from a review of AI's metastatic growth. "The last five years constitute a watershed moment in the history of AI," said Professor Sheila McIlraith, chair of the AI100 Standing Committee, in a statement. " This report examines what led to the extraordinary capabilities of today's AI systems, and how they are reshaping society. As we look ahead, we anticipate continued increase in AI capabilities alongside transformative advances in science and medicine. "Rapid change will challenge governments and industry to support and safeguard our people, our institutions, and our critical infrastructure. Both the benefits and the risks of AI technologies require the same clear-eyed scrutiny." Established in 2014, the One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100) is overseen by a Standing Committee of AI experts and administered by Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI). It's charged with producing reports every five years, the first of which debuted in 2016. The 2026 report's other key points highlight the transformation brought about by increasingly capable machine learning software. It identifies scaling as the engine of AI's advance, but also points to the growing cost and difficulty of obtaining training data as constraints on further progress. The report likens AI's disruptive potential to that of the World Wide Web – without dwelling on the irony that the web itself is among the things being disrupted. It points to creative industries, computer programming, and mathematics as fields once deemed beyond the reach of automation that are now being upended. Science, the report says, is being transformed by AI as it accelerates research timelines and opens up novel challenges. At the same time, the report cautions that "we will need to understand how AI-mediated information environments reshape collective cognition and moral behavior." The recent retraction of some 1,400 scholarly papers for failure to meet academic standards highlights the urgency of that message. Then there's the AI investment boom and "fears of a financial bubble, " which won't be assuaged by recent NASDAQ volatility and revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged intelligence operative for China. Concerns about the concentration of frontier AI development, the pressure AI puts on cybersecurity, and the active use of AI for military applications are also noted in the report. So too are worries about what AI-generated media does to trust. Item nine on

item.title: See the first images from the new ZWO Seestar S30 Plus — a smart telescope aimed at beginners
item.description: null As rival makers announce increasingly ambitious smart telescopes , ZWO has taken a different approach. Its new Seestar S30 Plus launched today and is available for $474 from Seestar’s website and Amazon , just in time for Christmas. Better still, we’ve been using it for a month and can bring you a first look. Announced a few months after the flagship Seestar S50 Pro and replacing the now-discontinued Seestar S30 , the new Seestar S30 Plus retains its 30mm aperture and compact chassis, but upgrades to four-element apochromatic optics with extra-low dispersion (ED) glass and two 3.7-megapixel cameras. The ZWO Seestar S30 Plus is a new sub-$500 smart telescope with upgraded optics and dual 3.7MP cameras. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Seestar S30 Plus: was $499 now $474 It has a 1.2-inch (30 mm) aperture, two 3.7 MP cameras and four-element apochromatic optics bundled into a compact build. View Deal Both produce 1,440 x 2,560-pixel images, while a much-improved 43.5-degree wide-angle camera can capture the Milky Way , constellations , star trails and nightscapes. Built-in filters, a mosaic mode and equatorial (EQ) tracking add considerable deep-sky astrophotography potential. For a telescope weighing just 3.64 lbs (1.65 kg), it’s impressive. It easily fits into a camera bag and could happily live on a bookshelf. The Seestar S30 Plus weighs just 3.64 lbs (1.65 kg) and fits in a camera bag easily. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) I’ve already photographed the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) , the Pleiades (M45) , the Dumbbell Nebula (M27) and the North America Nebula (NGC 7000). The results are excellent for such a small instrument, especially when imaging nebulas with its built-in dual-band filter, which helps reduce light pollution. The Seestar app adds new in-app post-processing options, so you don’t have to mess around with any of that — though you can also export everything as lossless FITS files. The S30 Plus also includes a magnetic solar filter, enabling you to indulge in solar photography safely. The North America Nebula (NGC 7000), the Pleiades (M45) and a star trail imaged using the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) With Dwarflab’s $1,299 Draco (3.5-inch/90mm aperture) recently landed in stores and Vaonis’ own $4,990 Atlas (3.1-inch/80mm aperture) not available until 2027, ZWO’s decision to offer an upgraded entry-level smart telescope that buyers can get their hands on right now looks particularly smart. The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) With ZWO's pattern of delivering cheaper smart telescopes without sacrificing on quality, the Seestar S30 Plus could be one of Christmas 2026’s best gifts for anyone interested in astronomy — and maybe that’s the point of it. Either way, first impressions are good. A full review is coming tomorrow, so check back at Space.com to find out our full thoughts and testing.

item.title: Why an Instagram Following Tracker Can Reveal More Than a Profile’s Follower Count
item.description: A popular Instagram account can attract thousands of followers, but that number rarely tells the whole story. For businesses, content creators, and people researching social media trends, another question can be just as interesting: which accounts does that person choose to follow? Someone may publicly promote fashion, technology, or entertainment while following creators in entirely different fields. A business account may begin following emerging influencers long before announcing a collaboration. A public figure may gradually change the types of accounts appearing on their Following list. These observations can provide useful context, particularly when viewed over time. An Instagram following tracker helps organize changes to the accounts a public Instagram profile follows. Rather than relying on a single snapshot, tools such as Snoopreport record detected follows and unfollows across reporting periods. The results can support social media research, although they cannot explain why someone followed an account or reveal information that Instagram keeps private. Why Follower Counts Don’t Tell the Whole Story Follower numbers are among Instagram’s most visible statistics. They influence how people assess popularity, reach, and sometimes commercial value. Yet having a large audience doesn’t necessarily mean an account has a clearly defined set of interests or strong connections within a particular industry. The Following list offers a different perspective. Consider a technology commentator who starts following several artificial intelligence researchers, software companies, and digital policy organizations. Those additions may suggest topics worth investigating. Similarly, a lifestyle influencer who follows numerous local restaurants might be exploring a new content category. Neither example proves a professional plan or future collaboration. Following someone can reflect curiosity, personal connections, or temporary interest. Still, when researchers compare several observations across time, they may discover changes worth examining further. The Difference Between Following and Followers Before using an Instagram following tracker, it’s important to distinguish two commonly confused terms. Followers are people who subscribe to an account’s updates. Following refers to the accounts that the profile has chosen to follow. For example, a creator may have 40,000 followers while following only 600 accounts. A following tracker focuses on changes within those 600 connections, not on identifying people who recently followed the creator. Instagram allows users to inspect the Following list of an accessible public profile. However, the list doesn’t provide a dependable chronological history of when each connection was added. The order in which accounts appear should not be treated as a reliable record of recent follows. To understand changes, the list needs to be observed across different periods. item.title: What an Instagram Likes Viewer Can Tell Us About the Content People Enjoy
item.description: People reveal different sides of themselves on Instagram. Their profiles may feature carefully selected photographs, polished videos, and short biographies, but their everyday interactions with content can tell another story. A person who rarely posts about travel may regularly like photographs of unfamiliar destinations. A creator known for fashion might engage with technology tutorials, food videos, or sports content. These interactions can suggest topics that attract someone’s attention, even when they don’t appear on the person’s own profile. An Instagram likes viewer can help organize detected likes from public accounts, making it easier to identify recurring content themes rather than examining isolated posts. However, likes are an imperfect signal. They may indicate enjoyment, curiosity, support, or simply a momentary reaction. Understanding their limitations is essential before drawing conclusions. Why Instagram Likes Are So Interesting A like is one of the simplest interactions on social media. It takes only a moment, but it can reflect many different motivations. Someone might like a photograph because they admire the subject, appreciate the photography, support a friend, or agree with a message. For content creators and marketers, likes also form part of the wider picture of audience engagement. A beauty influencer may notice that certain makeup tutorials attract more engagement than product announcements. A restaurant could discover that behind-the-scenes videos generate stronger reactions than ordinary menu photographs. These observations can guide content decisions, especially when combined with comments, shares, reach, and other performance metrics. But there is an important difference between analyzing engagement on your own posts and studying what a particular public account likes elsewhere. Instagram makes the first task relatively straightforward. The second is more complicated. Can You See What Someone Likes on Instagram? Instagram lets users inspect the likes associated with individual posts they can access. For example, if a public photograph has received likes, its visible engagement information may show which accounts interacted with it. What Instagram doesn’t provide is a single public page listing all the posts another person has liked. The platform removed its old Following Activity tab in 2019. That feature previously offered a window into some activities of accounts people followed. Today, users can still explore publicly visible interactions, but building a comprehensive history of another account’s likes is not a standard Instagram feature. This is why an Instagram likes viewer is different from simply opening a photograph and checking its engagement. A viewer attempts to gather detectable likes associated with a selected account and present them together across reporting periods. What Can Repeated Likes Suggest? One liked photograph rarely provides meaningful evidence about someone’s broader interests. Imagine a pu

item.title: A science fiction novel has finally won the Booker prize. It’s about time
item.description: M. John Harrison is considered the first bona fide science fiction author to win the Booker prize Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP/Alamy Back in June, our science fiction columnist Emily H. Wilson made a bold claim : M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything was not only “the best science-fiction book of the year so far”, but also a “wholly original… work of genius”. Not only has Emily been proved right, but perhaps she didn’t go quite far enough. This story of an alien invasion won the Booker prize last night, making it – in the Booker judges’ opinion, at least – not just the best science fiction book of the year so far, but the best novel in any genre of the year. Read more These two new sci-fi novels really impressed us It’s about time. Back in 2009, the great Kim Stanley Robinson – another writer of genius, in my opinion – wrote a piece for New Scientist in which he argued that “three or four of the last 10 Booker prizes should have gone to science fiction novels the juries hadn’t read”. With remarkable prescience, Robinson even tipped Harrison’s Signs of Life as one of those books. Advertisement There has been a long-running reluctance in the literary world to allow science fiction (often abbreviated to SF) into the starry ranks of so-called “literary” fiction. As Harrison himself told the BBC’s Front Row last month, he has “been working for 40 to 50 years to shift the balance, both as a novelist and as a critic… Why shouldn’t a well written SF be considered to be literary fiction?”. His win is being trumpeted today as the first time a science fiction novel has won the Booker prize. I’d quibble a little with that – how about Margaret Atwood’s The Testaments , the sequel to The Handmaid’s Tale , set in a dystopian version of the US, which was 2019’s winner? She’d likely quibble with me in return: Atwood has a lot to say about the difference between science fiction and speculative fiction, defining her Gilead stories firmly as the latter. Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter But this very unwillingness to define a novel as science fiction speaks to that long-running literary snobbery. As the late, great Ursula K. Le Guin put it, reviewing Atwood’s The Year of the Flood back in 2009: “She doesn’t want the literary bigots to shove her into the literary ghetto.” Whether or not Harrison is the first science fiction author to win the Booker, it’s definitely the case that, as Booker Prize Foundation chief executive Gaby Wood put it in the prize announcement: “Many past Booker Prize authors have borrowed facets of science fiction in their work, but M. John Harrison is the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world.” And this means, I hope, that our days of looking down on science fiction are over. item.title: Chrome zero-day whack-a-mole continues as 2026 tally hits 8
item.description: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar. The latest flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, is a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome's XML component. Google confirmed in a security advisory published Monday that attackers are already exploiting the bug, although it hasn't said who's behind the attacks or who might be getting targeted. "Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said, offering little else about the attacks. The vulnerability was reported anonymously on November 6 and involves a memory management error that occurs when software continues using a pointer to memory that has already been freed. Such bugs can potentially allow attackers to corrupt memory and execute malicious code, although Google hasn't disclosed how this particular flaw is being exploited. Google is keeping further technical details under wraps until enough users have installed the fix, a familiar approach intended to stop other attackers from getting their hands on a working exploit. The patch arrives in Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update also addresses eight other security vulnerabilities, including high-severity flaws affecting WebGL, FileSystem, GPU, Compositing, and the V8 JavaScript engine. The release fixes another use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component, CVE-2026-125346, which was reported by Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security in October, though Google hasn't indicated that this second vulnerability is being exploited. The latest discovery adds to what's becoming a rather long list of Chrome zero-days this year. By June, Google had already patched five actively exploited Chrome zero-days , including flaws in its V8 JavaScript engine, Skia graphics library, and WebGPU implementation. The list has only grown since then, with two more V8 bugs fixed in September and the latest XML vulnerability bringing the total to eight. That puts 2026 level with 2025, when Google also fixed eight Chrome zero-days exploited in the wild. Whether the browser maker can make it through the remaining weeks of the year without adding another to the pile is anyone's guess. Google says the latest update will roll out over the coming days and weeks, but users can check manually by heading to Chrome's Settings menu and selecting About Chrome. With attackers already making use of the vulnerability, it's probably worth doing that sooner rather than waiting for Chrome to get around to it. ®

item.title: Ransomware threat blares from Vanderbilt University computers during cyberattack
item.description: Classes at Vanderbilt University are proceeding as scheduled today, although access to most university systems remains restricted following a cyberattack claimed by ransomware group BYOD. Vanderbilt announced on Monday morning that it was dealing with "an active cybersecurity incident," and that the fallout may affect university devices, systems, and cloud-based services. The Nashville-based university initially told students and staff to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi. It warned them to watch for unexpected prompts, altered files or permissions, unfamiliar applications, and unsolicited authentication requests. Campus computers reportedly began playing an audio threat attributed to BYOD. Student newspaper The Vanderbilt Hustler cited posts on campus social network Fizz showing the message. "You have been compromised by BYOD," the recording said. "We suggest you reach out to us as soon as possible. Instructions have been placed on your desktop. Failure to communicate will result in this estate being brought to the ground completely. Make the right choice or rot with the wrong one." By Monday evening, Vanderbilt had restored access to campus Wi-Fi, but warned that access to most systems remains restricted. "We know this has disrupted important work and caused frustration across the university," it said . "Vanderbilt Information Technology is working with government agencies and other partners to manage this situation." Students were told to attend classes as scheduled on Tuesday and contact instructors about flexibility on coursework deadlines. Staff were instructed to report to work normally. Vanderbilt's Athletics department said that its ticketing system was unavailable, and that students were unable to claim tickets for the college's football game against Alabama on Saturday. BYOD claimed responsibility for the attack on Vanderbilt on Monday, along with extensive data theft. "If you could not tell already, your databases are locked [and] we have your entire estate and research data," it said via its leak site. "Over 1 million SSNs, full names, email addresses, phone numbers, student and employee records, full takeover of your DC, whatever was on your network, we possess." Vanderbilt has not confirmed BYOD's claims about the extent of its access or the data allegedly stolen. BYOD may be a familiar name to some. The group previously claimed attacks on the University of New Mexico and Trump Mobile's customer database . BYOD also claimed responsibility on Monday for an attack on Texas Health and Human Services. The agency has not publicly confirmed an incident and did not immediately respond to our questions. ®

item.title: Total solar eclipse 2027 vs 2028 — Which one should you choose, Egypt or Australia?
item.description: null For those who want to experience a total solar eclipse, the next two years present the best kind of problem. On Aug. 2, 2027, the so-called "eclipse of the century " will sweep across southern Spain, North Africa and the Middle East, bringing more than six minutes of totality to parts of Egypt. Then, on July 22, 2028, another exceptionally long total solar eclipse will cross Australia, putting the remote Outback and Sydney Harbor in the path of the moon's dark central shadow before it reaches New Zealand's beautiful South Island. Both eclipses will be spectacular, and both will require careful planning, yet they promise very different experiences. The 2027 event combines over six minutes of totality with some of the very best weather prospects possible, while 2028 offers over five minutes of totality above some of the world's most famous wildernesses and cityscapes. Eclipse chasing requires careful planning and dedication, but also significant funds. If you can only choose one, which should it be? 2027 total solar eclipse: pros and cons A map of the 2027 total solar eclipse path. (Image credit: Michael Zeiler/EclipseAtlas.com) On paper, 2027 is difficult to beat. Maximum totality on Aug. 2 will last about 6 minutes, 23 seconds, making it the longest totality on land since 1991 and until 2114. The path of totality will cross southern Spain and Gibraltar before sweeping across Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, Sudan, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Somalia and the Chagos Islands. About 88.9 million people live in its path, according to Time and Date . It will dominate the news for weeks. For Europeans, southern Spain is the obvious easy option. Tarifa, at the country's southern tip, will see about 4 minutes, 39 seconds of totality, while the U.K. Overseas Territory of Gibraltar gets about 4 minutes, 25 seconds. Travel farther east and the duration increases, with Sfax in Tunisia getting around 5 minutes, 41 seconds and locations in Egypt experiencing more than six minutes. Weather prospects generally improve, too, as the path crosses the deserts of North Africa. Egypt is the headline destination. Luxor will see about 6 minutes, 20 seconds of totality near midday, with Karnak Temple, the Valley of the Kings, and some of the world's greatest ancient monuments nearby. The climatic odds are excellent, with clouds extremely rare in early August. That combination of a very long totality, ancient landscapes and a very high probability of a clear sky makes 2027's path of totality highly unusual. But there are downsides. Temperatures around Luxor can exceed 105°F (41°C) in August, a dust storm is not impossible, and totality occurs shortly after 1 p.m. when the sun (and moon) will be high overhead — making photography very difficult. Demand is already intense, making organized trips expensive. Spain will be considerably easier and probably cheaper for European eclipse chasers, but at the expense of roughly two minutes of totality — and slightly less favora

item.title: How Heineken Created Immersive Experiences That Took Lagos Fashion Week 2026 Beyond the Runway
item.description: In a city where creativity is a culture and every corner has a story to tell, Heineken brought another expression of Lagos to life at Lagos Fashion Week 2026 . Through its City of Cities: Where Taste Rules experience, the brand transformed its eleven-year partnership with the fashion showcase into a celebration of the people, ideas, and experiences shaping the city’s creative identity, bringing fashion, music, innovation, and social connections together across the week. From runway presentations to the Heineken Lounge, the debut of Heineken Studio, and an energetic after-party, the brand created experiences that went beyond the collections on display, inviting guests to explore new expressions of taste, discover creative possibilities, and connect over shared interests. At the heart of the experience was City of Cities: Where Taste Rules, an experience inspired by the many influences that make Lagos what it is. First introduced in 2025, the concept recognises that Lagos is more than one city; it is a melting pot of different cultures, communities, sounds, and styles. At Lagos Fashion Week 2026, Heineken brought this idea into focus, celebrating the diversity of expression that makes the city’s creative scene distinct. The experience also marked another chapter in Heineken’s eleven-year journey with Lagos Fashion Week. Over the years, the partnership has explored the intersection of fashion, craftsmanship, and taste through initiatives such as Woven Threads in 2022, the Dyelab collaboration in 2023, and the H45 Collection in 2024, before introducing City of Cities: Where Taste Rules in 2025. Each edition has created a new way to engage with fashion and culture, with this year’s experience building on that foundation through fresh expressions of creativity and innovation. Aligned with the 2026 theme, CRAFTED: Heritage. Innovation. Circular Futures, Heineken’s presence celebrated the artistry, intentionality, and evolving perspectives shaping contemporary fashion. Across the venue, guests arrived in style, adding their own interpretations of fashion and self-expression to the atmosphere. The Heineken Lounge provided a space to unwind, exchange ideas, and connect as guests enjoyed chilled Heineken, refreshments, and the runway presentations. The experience also offered a taste of something different, with guests exploring Foam Infusions in exciting variations, including espresso and blood orange. A major highlight was the Nigerian debut of Heineken Studio, the brand’s Playground of Innovation, which brought together taste, creativity, and personal expression in an interactive space. Beyond discovering new ways to experience lager through Foam Infusions, guests could step into the painting studio to create personalised designs on their own Heineken cans. The photo area and Heineken-branded backdrops also became popular spots for guests to capture their moments, express their individual styles, and share their experiences. item.title: Smart meters to cost the UK billions: 2G switch-off means replacing 12-13 million
item.description: Between 12 and 13 million UK smart meters could stop working properly when 2G and 3G networks are switched off by 2033, and replacing them all is likely to cost around £4 billion ($5.3 billion). Smart meters have long been a controversial topic thanks to the British government's botched rollout of the technology; they were supposed to be fitted into 80 percent of households by 2020. But numerous delays and technical hitches, such as consumers finding their meter stopped being smart if they switched energy supplier , hindered progress. Now, a report from connectivity biz Wirepas, "The European Connectivity Trilemma," shows that it isn't just Brits who have problems, but that other European countries also have their share of smart meter issues and that no two countries have adopted the same approach. The UK's issues center on the fact that early meters used 2G or 3G cellular connections to transmit energy usage back to the supplier. These continued to be fitted until 4G versions began arriving at the end of 2024, the report says. This issue was covered by The Register back in 2023 , and again in 2024 . However, the government had already announced measures to phase out 2G and 3G networks by 2033 several years earlier, back in 2021, so it was known that any meters being fitted would have a limited lifespan. In fact, 3G services have now already been withdrawn by the networks , and they all plan to phase out 2G ahead of the 2033 deadline . BT/EE will begin closing its network from May 2029, VMO2 will start the same summer, and Vodafone aims to switch off in spring 2030. The report claims the UK now faces two substantial areas of expenditure as a result. The first covers newer, second generation (SMETS2) meters, where only the communications module needs swapping out, but even this is likely to cost £1.3 to £1.4 billion (c $1.7 to $1.9 billion) before the hardware cost of each new hub is even factored in. The other is for an estimated 7 million older, first-generation (SMETS1) meter installations, which have the cellular comms hard-wired in, so the whole meter typically needs replacing. The report authors estimate this will cost another £2.1 billion to £2.45 billion ($2.8 billion to $3.3 billion), at an indicative replacement cost of £300 to £350 per installation. This results in the estimated £4 billion in gross replacement costs, which will ultimately feed into household energy bills, adding to the very costs the government is currently trying to reduce. We asked the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), which oversees smart meters, for comment. A spokesperson said: "Smart meters are already helping millions of consumers manage their energy and save money on bills," they told The Reg . "The transition to 4G is a planned upgrade that will continue to deliver the benefits that smart meters already provide to households and industry." item.title: Ukraine’s fiber-optic drones get squeezed by AI data center demand
item.description: Impervious to battlefield jamming, drones physically connected to human operators by miles of fiber-optic cables have become such a common weapon of war in Ukraine that trees and fields are strewn with tangled cables thinner than fishing lines. But importing such fiber-optic material from China has become more costly as drone warfare’s needs compete with global demand from AI data centers for the same limited supply—and so Ukrainian drone makers have been adapting. Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, the Ukrainians have been forced out of necessity to continually develop battlefield innovations involving first-person view (FPV) quadcopter drones and other heavier types of drones. But it was the Russian military that first deployed unjammable fiber-optic drones to repel Ukrainian forces’ cross-border incursion into the Kursk Oblast in 2024. The Ukrainians quickly followed suit in developing their own fiber-optic drones, given the drones’ capability to shrug off electronic warfare jamming that could neutralize radio-controlled drones. Russia and Ukraine have relied on Chinese suppliers for some off-the-shelf drones and a wide array of drone components, including bulk orders of fiber wound around very large spools or sometimes small finished spools ready for installation on drones. The finished spools can hold enough fiber-optic cable for drones to regularly operate at ranges of dozens of miles, and sometimes up to 62 miles (100 kilometers) in extreme cases, as reported by the independent Russian publication The Insider . item.title: Review: Apple's M6 MacBook Pro is good, but it's missing all the exciting stuff
item.description: I've written more than once about the weird positioning of Apple's entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro, which has always occupied an uncomfortable perch between the MacBook Air and the higher-end MacBook Pros. The best versions of this laptop, like last year's M5 refresh, come with the same basic design and external features of the higher-end MacBook Pros, just with a more modest processor and a lower ceiling for specs like RAM and storage. The lesser versions stick with older designs or other compromises, reserving Apple's most updated designs and screen technologies for the more expensive high-end models. Recall the 13-inch M1 and M2 MacBook Pros, which stuck with Apple's 2016-era MacBook Pro designs for everything , up to and including the now-abandoned Touch Bar. (If you're someone at Apple maintaining Touch Bar support into the 2030s for the sake of these two laptop models, I'd like to hear from you. Not for a story! I'd just like to know how you are.) This year's entry-level MacBook Pro mostly falls into that latter category. It does get an Apple M6 chip, and the M6 is great—rumors suggest the M6 won't get Pro, Max, or Ultra configurations, so there are some fringe benefits here that you can't get in the top-tier MacBook Pros. But it uses the same MacBook Pro design Apple has been using since 2021 . There's no touchscreen, no OLED panel, no Dynamic Island, no half-pound weight reduction, no glowing Apple logo on the lid. item.title: Google DeepMind melds humans and AI agents to vet Signal's secure messaging techniques
item.description: Google DeepMind researchers have completed a formal verification of Signal's messaging security, marking what they claim is the first time AI has helped devise a proof that links protocol-level security guarantees to a widely used cryptographic implementation. They did so using AlphaProof Code, a multi-agent framework for formal software specification and verification. AlphaProof Code relies on a human-guided agent that writes a Lean specification, assesses machine code semantics, and crafts an agent-authored proof that the Lean kernel checks against the specification. In this instance, AlphaProof Code verified Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet , thereby validating the design of libsignal 's forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy. In so doing, the Google/DeepMind team – Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli – has taken a step toward a challenge the Beneficial AI Foundation issued in April to formally verify the Signal protocol and Signal app with Lean. The AlphaProof Code process involves working with various models to turn Signal's security goals into a human-reviewed mathematical specification. Based on this spec, the researchers assigned Gemini Carbon agents to generate Lean code proving the correctness of the libsignal implementation. After the agents generated 6.5 million lines of Lean code, they undertook an auditing pass and flagged bits that required human review. The result is theoretical in that it assumes perfect cryptography and doesn't guarantee the computational secrecy of bytes. But it's still a meaningful assertion of correctness. "It's a system that is fundamentally built for human AI collaboration," said Swarat Chaudhuri, research scientist at Google DeepMind and a professor at the University of Texas at Austin, in an interview with The Register . Traditionally, said Chaudhuri, you start proving theorems with well-defined problems formulated by a mathematician that get submitted to an AI agent for proof. In this case, the researchers had to figure out what to prove. "In formal methods, we always had this belief that verification is the hard bit," he said. "There's thirty or forty years of work on how to scale up verification. Now we are able to do that. So now the question is what are we verifying? … That process is fundamentally human-in-the-loop, but we devised a process of trying to scale it up to the extent possible with AI." As Chaudhuri and his colleagues note in their research paper, "AlphaProof Code: Verifying Signal’s Security at the Machine-Code Level," formal verification used to require heroic efforts. Formally verifying the seL4 microkernel took 20 person-years, while developing the verified CompCert C compiler took six years. AlphaProof Code, they believe, can drastically reduce the cost of formal verification, though their Signal work still took

item.title: Microsoft is giving Claude the keys to UK Copilot tenants by default
item.description: Microsoft will enable access to Anthropic's Claude models by default for UK Copilot tenants next month, giving administrators a deadline to decide whether US-based processing fits their compliance requirements. From December 9, UK tenants whose administrators have not already chosen a setting will have Claude access enabled. Administrators can disable it, but leaving the setting untouched means opting in. In this instance, Anthropic operates as a Microsoft subprocessor , and Claude models are already on by default for most customers in the Windows giant's commercial cloud. The exceptions, notably, include the European Union, the European Free Trade Association, and the UK. However, UK tenants aren't in scope for Microsoft's EU Data Boundary - launched at the start of 2023 - and so Redmond is flipping the switch for the country. Anthropic processes the relevant data in the United States, Microsoft's documentation states . Administrators therefore have until December 9 to review whether that meets their organization's data-handling requirements and set access accordingly. Microsoft is also retiring the setting that restricts Claude access to Microsoft 365 alone. "This affirms Microsoft's commitment to offering choice between leading AI models while maintaining enterprise-grade security and compliance," the Redmond-based biz said. So long as you don't mind processing happening in the US. ®

item.title: EU's €212M border IT project lands IBM and Atos in legal water
item.description: The European Union has dragged IBM, Atos, and Leonardo into court over years of delays to its troubled €212 million smart border system, which finally went live after missing a string of deadlines and leaving travelers stuck in airport queues. The lawsuit dates back to December 22, 2025, when eu-LISA, the agency behind the EU's fingerprint-and-facial-image border checks for non-EU travelers, filed its claim in an Estonian court. The lawsuit was buried in eu-LISA's 2025 financial accounts , published in July, with no mention of who was being sued. The Financial Times has since named the three companies after obtaining letters exchanged with the agency. In a statement to The Register , eu-LISA confirmed it had initiated proceedings "in line with the Agency’s responsibility to protect the EU’s financial interests." "The proceedings concern the system’s development phase and have no impact on its current operation. EES (entry exit system) is fully operational," the agency said, declining to discuss the ongoing case. The EES was supposed to be ready in 2022 yet wasn't live until October 2025 and was only fully operational from April. Travelers have since had to contend with hours-long airport queues and fingerprint scanners that reportedly struggle with sweaty fingers. Behind the scenes, things weren't going much better, with the consortium and eu-LISA spending years arguing over missed deadlines, financial penalties and who was to blame. IBM Belgium and Atos Belgium were already arguing over penalties back in October 2021, when they disputed a fine from eu-LISA and pointed to the COVID-19 pandemic and other factors beyond their control as reasons for the delays. By February 2022, the consortium was pushing back against another set of deadlines, warning that the agency's timetable was unrealistic. "Ignoring reality is not prudent and will not help to achieve the plan," the companies wrote, according to the FT. "On the contrary, working with an unrealistic plan will cause frustration for all stakeholders." The consortium also criticized eu-LISA's "overall governance," suggesting relations between the two sides had become rather frosty. The fallout wasn't cheap. The contract had already grown from €142 million to €212 million in 2021, and the delays kept adding to the bill. In its 2022 accounts [PDF], eu-LISA acknowledged difficulties with the consortium and warned of additional costs, with the setbacks also holding up other EU IT projects. By 2023, it had nearly doubled its annual EES budget to €40 million by diverting funds from elsewhere, partly to cover rising hardware and software maintenance costs. The FT also reported that IBM agreed in March 2022 to let eu-LISA withhold certain payments while the dispute over damages was resolved. The original contract expired last year, with a new consortium taking over implementation, although IBM, Atos, and Leonardo remained responsible until August. item.title: NASA's twin ESCAPADE Mars probes slingshot around Earth in unprecedented double 'gravity assist'
item.description: null Twin NASA spacecraft are wrapping up a year-long escapade, ready to make a beeline to the Red Planet. The Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers (ESCAPADE) spacecraft launched in November 2025 on the second-ever flight of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket. But rather than head straight to Mars, the two spacecraft dawdled through a looping trajectory . Now, they are back in Earth's neighborhood where they tackled a crucial engine burn unusually close to Earth that — if all goes well — will set them on track for Mars . "No NASA mission has ever done this before," said Rob Lillis, a planetary and space physicist at the University of California, Berkeley and principal investigator of the ESCAPADE mission. "For most missions, it just isn't necessary." That's because traditionally NASA's Mars missions have been carefully choreographed within cosmic launch constraints, leaving Earth during a brief window of planetary alignment that only occurs every 26 months. ESCAPADE was meant to launch in October 2024, when Earth and Mars were favorably aligned, but delays with the New Glenn rocket forced the mission to sit out the precious launch window. Rather than wait to launch this fall, NASA decided to try something new. ESCAPADE mission planners designed a "loitering" orbit , shaped like a kidney bean. It called for the twin probes to loop through that trajectory to be back at Earth in early November 2026, ready to continue on to Mars. The ESCAPADE mission's unique path to reach Mars. After launching in November 2025, the twin ESCAPADE probes looped around the Earth-Sun Lagrange point 2 (L2), in a "loiter" orbit that returned them to Earth in November 2026 where they used our planet's gravity to slingshot themselves to Mars. (Image credit: Advanced Space/Matt Bolliger) Once they arrived, however, the twin probes faced a major hurdle: Each had to perfectly execute an engine burn within Earth's gravity well. The maneuver is similar to the slingshot flybys that spacecraft regularly conduct to adjust their trajectories — but here, the probes had to fire their engines to amp up the effect of the burn rather than acting alone. The first spacecraft tackled the feat on Nov. 7; the second did so on Monday (Nov. 9). And according to NASA, the burns went perfectly. "This is the first time NASA has used a powered Earth flyby to propel a spacecraft toward Mars, and we've now executed this maneuver twice, flawlessly, in just two days," Asal Naseri, acting associate flight director for NASA's Heliophysics Division said in a statement . After just a few minor course corrections, ESCAPADE will be sailing toward a September 2027 Mars arrival. A scenic detour The twin ESCAPADE spacecraft have made the most of their extended tour. Each spacecraft is about the size of two refrigerators and equipped with three scientific instruments and a couple cameras. item.title: 5 New Albums to Listen to This Week: Skepta, Phyno, Ty Bello & More
item.description: Skepta holding the official clear vinyl edition of his sixth studio album, The Fork and Knife. Photo Credit: Skepta/Instagram Your playlist could do with a little shake-up, and these five albums might be exactly what it needs. Skepta is reconnecting with his roots, Phyno is giving us more of the indigenous rap we love, Ty Bello has two albums exploring different expressions of worship, and Anendlessocean and Tobe Nwigwe are taking their sounds in interesting directions. From UK grime and Nigerian hip-hop to alternative gospel and soul, there’s a lot to discover across these new releases. Whether you’re in the mood for bars, worship, thoughtful songwriting or music that brings different cultures together, this week’s selection has something worth hearing. Skepta: The Fork & Knife Back in 2012, Skepta found himself at odds with a corporatised grime scene, sparking a pivotal career reckoning that eventually led to his landmark 2016 album Konnichiwa. On his long-awaited 15-track sixth album, The Fork & Knife, the 44-year-old MC reflects on his journey as grime’s most influential elder statesman and the son of Nigerian immigrants. Named after his mother’s favourite proverb, the record is a deep exploration of identity and perseverance. Musically, Skepta bridges continents by blending global diasporic sounds. He teams up with Aya Nakamura on the zouk-infused “ Chippie ”, taps Asake for the Afrobeats crossover “ Aloe Vera ”, and recruits Chase & Status alongside Suggs for the sharp single “ Innocent Smile ”. The project closes with “ Belly ”, an eight-minute masterclass featuring Boy Better Know members Jme and Frisco . ﻿ Phyno: Let That Sink In Arriving nearly 10 years after his groundbreaking sophomore record The Playmaker, Phyno’s 15-track sixth solo album, Let That Sink In (LTSI), showcases his timeless command of indigenous rap. Across the record,the Enugu-born star blends soul, R&B, and traditional Nigerian sounds to explore faith, resilience, and personal evolution. The album features powerhouse collaborations, including Seyi Vibez on the opener “ Ndu Ka Aku ”, Fireboy DML on “ I Believe ”, and Jeriq on “ Ije Enu ”. Whether taking the government to task on “20 Years to Come” or offering uplifting anthems like “ Chukwu Okike ”, Phyno proves why he remains a definitive voice in African hip-hop. ﻿ Ty Bello: I Speak Lion and I Speak Lamb Creative powerhouse Ty Bello delivers a massive double-album listening experience with I Speak Lion and I Speak Lamb . Split into two distinct spiritual volumes, the expansive project captures both the bold, triumphant authority of worship and its quiet, intimate moments. ﻿ I Speak Lion leans into explosive, high-energy sounds designed to spark courage, featuring powerful pairings with Sunmisola Agbebi , Greatman Takit , and Limoblaze . In contrast, I Speak Lamb steps into soaking acoustic textures and tender devotional spaces, offering a complete, multi-layered sanctuary for listeners. ﻿ Anendlessocean: Freedom Alte

item.title: Ifeyinwa Azubike Reconsiders the Rules of Dressing with The Ladymaker’s Stand On Ceremony
item.description: During Lagos Fashion Week, The Ladymaker ’s Founder and Creative Director, Ifeyinwa Azubike, introduced Stand On Ceremony, a collection that considers the relationship between personal expression and the expectations attached to an occasion. Presented on 27 October 2026 at The Sphere, Lagos, the collection draws from the familiar expression to stand on ceremony: to insist on the observance of formalities. For Ifeyinwa Azubike, the idea presents an opportunity to examine the traditions women inherit, the rituals they observe and the choices they make when dressing for themselves. The collection is built around two identities: The Devotee and The Rebel. They are not opposing personalities so much as two ways of relating to ceremony. The Devotee embraces its rituals. She understands the language of formal dressing and participates in it with intention. For her, dressing fully is an expression of desire and personal conviction. The Rebel is equally familiar with the rules, but she is selective about the ones she follows. Her approach to dressing allows for disruption, though never simply for the sake of attention. Through these characters, Azubike considers a familiar experience for women: the pull between what an occasion expects and what an individual wants to express. Every woman who has dressed for an occasion has encountered this tension in some form, whether in choosing to honour a tradition or finding room to express herself within it. The garments give form to this conversation. The Cloister Dress is paired with the Banner Dress, while the Manor Jumpsuit is placed alongside the Assembly Set. Other looks, including the Herald Dress, Emissary Set, Procession Dress and Sovereign Set, extend the collection’s exploration of the two identities. Material choices move between crimson jacquard, rose jacquard, ice jacquard, denim Akwete, wine Adire, midnight sequins and beaded velvet. The collection draws on fabrics and textures that allow ceremony to be interpreted through different moods, silhouettes and degrees of formality. Stand On Ceremony was presented during Lagos Fashion Week through an intimate fashion presentation, followed by a soirée where guests could experience the garments more closely. The evening was held in partnership with MAC Cosmetics, which provided beauty; Moët & Chandon, the champagne partner; Jacque Scents, which created the fragrance experience; and The Nail Boutique , responsible for nail artistry. For Ifeyinwa Azubike, the question the collection leaves with its audience is a personal one: are you a Rebel or a Devotee? The Ladymaker Brand Profile Founded in 2015 by Ifeyinwa Azubike, The Ladymaker is a Lagos-based womenswear brand that brings together African heritage, classical elegance and contemporary design. Established by Azubike following a career in commercial law, the brand was born from a desire to create timeless clothing rooted in craftsmanship, fit and enduring style rather than fleeting trends. item.title: Leo StaEkeh Tells Women Leaders at TIWLC, Dubai: I Chose ‘Corporate Suicide’ Over the Safe Path
item.description: Africa’s tech icon and Chairman of Zinox Group , Leo Stan Ekeh , has told an international gathering of women leaders that his decision to build a technology company in Africa, at a time when the sector was virtually non-existent on the continent, amounted to what he described as “corporate suicide”. Speaking on the theme “Losing the Fear” , at The International Women Leadership Conference (TIWLC) in Dubai, organised by the Ibukun Awosika Leadership Foundation, Ekeh , who was a keynote speaker on the final day of this year’s conference, addressed over 600 women industry leaders from different countries across the globe. He said he returned from his studies abroad to a Nigeria where his peers were filing into banking, oil and gas, and where technology was largely seen as a foreign game. Ekeh, who studied Economics in India, said he was discouraged from pursuing a postgraduate degree in Computer Science in Europe because of the prevailing perception then that Africa might have little need for computers over the next 35 years, potentially leaving him frustrated. He subsequently opted for a postgraduate degree in Risk Management before pursuing a Master’s degree in Business Law (LLM) at London Guildhall University. He recalled that he could not sit his final law examinations because he had diverted his tuition fees into his passion for technology entrepreneurship. He also disclosed that he had fended off recruitment attempts by international technology companies that had sought to hire him before his return to Africa. “I chose the road not taken,” he told the conference. “It was corporate suicide in the eyes of my parents and many others. I lost the fear because I believed technology was the master key that would unlock possibilities for Nigeria and Africa.” He said the journey came with considerable hardship, including living on one meal a day for over three years and sleeping in a very small room in his office. According to him, his vision was to create a Nigerian and, by extension, an African IT identity. Recalling the launch of his first company, Task Systems Ltd, over 35 years ago, the company that pioneered desktop publishing and computer graphics in Nigeria. At the launch, held at the Sheraton Hotel, Ikeja, Ekeh recalled addressing an overcrowded hall filled with industry leaders, some of whom were seeing computers for the first time. He told them: “No country can claim to be independent without technology independence.” He said the Nigerian media embraced the vision, describing him as a “miracle child” and supporting the company’s roadmap. This, he noted, contributed to the computerisation of over 97 per cent of media and multimedia houses in Nigeria, as well as in other African countries. He further explained that the decision to establish Zinox Technologies, which became one of Africa’s first Microsoft WHQL- and Intel-certified computer manufacturers, was driven by the need to give Nigeria and Africa a global technology identity. “We were n

item.title: Midea Introduces Space Master Refrigerator in Nigeria, Bringing More Room to Everyday Living
item.description: Midea is introducing the Space Master Refrigerator to Nigerian consumers, placing practical food storage at the centre of its “More Room for Nigeria” campaign. The introduction speaks to a familiar household situation: a major grocery shop, a weekend of hosting or a family celebration can quickly turn refrigerator space into a daily planning challenge. Space Master is presented with a simple proposition: “Same Size. More Space. More Capacity.” Its approach to storage design gives households more usable interior space for the food, drinks and everyday essentials they need to keep at home. For households planning meals ahead, the practical question is not only what to buy, but where everything will go. Fresh produce, bottled drinks, ingredients for family meals and food prepared for guests all compete for space. Space Master’s bigger-capacity proposition gives consumers more room to accommodate larger grocery shops, everyday essentials and food for family occasions, helping households prepare more comfortably for both daily routines and celebrations. “ More Room for Nigeria” connects that functional product story to everyday Nigerian life. From stocking up for a busy working week to preparing for a family gathering, the campaign shows why usable storage matters at moments when households need flexibility. Its companion message, “Every Celebration Needs More Room,” gives the product a role in the preparations for the occasion — before guests arrive, meals are served and memories are made. The campaign also places product discovery at the heart of the consumer experience. Through planned retail demonstrations, shoppers will be invited to open the Space Master, explore its interior layout and see examples of how groceries and meal-preparation items can be arranged. The “Grocery Fit Challenge” and household grocery scenarios are designed to make the storage proposition tangible, while store representatives can answer model-specific questions and explain the purchase process. Midea ’s approach reflects a focus on applying product design and practical technology to everyday consumer needs. By making storage easier to visualize and explore, the brand aims to help shoppers evaluate how a refrigerator can suit their routines, household size and entertaining needs. Consumers interested in Space Master can enquire at authorized Midea retail outlets and request an in-store demonstration and confirmation of the specific model’s specifications, current stock availability and applicable purchase terms before making a decision. Executive Comment “In many homes, food storage becomes especially important when everyday routines meet the demands of hosting and celebration. With Space Master, we want consumers to experience how thoughtful refrigerator design can help them organize the things that matter to their households. ‘More Room for Nigeria’ brings that practical idea to life,” said Louis Zang, Home Appliances Sales Manager for Midea Nigeria. item.title: Royal Navy stands up first autonomous boat squadron
item.description: Britain’s Royal Navy has formally commissioned its first uncrewed boat squadron, operating seaborne drones on front-line operations as part of its “Hybrid Navy” strategy. The force says the 1 st Autonomous Squadron officially entered active service on November 5 at a ceremony in Portsmouth Naval Base. It comprises around 180 personnel, about the same as a Type 23 frigate, split into two watches to enable operations around the clock. This active squadron replaces Project Beehive, the navy’s experimental program to build a fleet of autonomous and remotely operated vessels, through which it obtained 20 uncrewed boats from UK-based Kraken Technology Group. The force is understood to be using both Kraken’s K3 Scout, and the SM400 from SYOS Aerospace, known by the Royal Navy as the Rattler. The K3 Scout is an 8.4 m boat capable of 55 knots and can carry a payload of up to 600 kg. It has a range of up to 650 nautical miles and endurance of up to 7 days. The maker describes it as capable of a range of missions, including anti-ship and anti-submarine to detecting and countering other drones and even casualty evacuation. The Rattler boat is 7.2 m and has a 500 kg modular bay, with a range of up to 950 nautical miles. It was used last year in a demonstration during which 5 of the uncrewed boats were remotely-piloted to escort patrol ship HMS Tyne and mine countermeasures mothership HMS Stirling Castle Part of the new squadron’s mission will be to act as pathfinder for drone operations, working on bringing additional types of uncrewed surface vessel (USVs) into fleet service and conducting a range of operations alongside other organizations – both as single vessels and as part of a task group. The “Hybrid Navy” concept was outlined by First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins earlier this year, who made the case that uncrewed vessels would be vital in filling the gaps left by the Royal Navy’s much depleted surface fleet. Speaking at the launch of the autonomous squadron, Fleet Commander Vice-Admiral Steve Moorhouse hailed it as an historic occasion, but warned that the seas are becoming more contested, more dangerous and harder to operate in. “A hybrid navy is about giving our people better tools. It means more reach, more striking power and more options,” he stated. Last week, the force also launched strike drones from one of its aircraft carriers for the first time. Nyan one-way drones made by BAE Systems were launched from the deck, as well as a Tekever AR5 fixed-wing uncrewed aircraft, the same kind the British Army has selected to replace its troublesome Watchkeeper fleet. item.title: Microsoft teaches schools that free email was just a phase
item.description: Microsoft is retiring its free education email service, leaving schools, colleges, and universities facing new licensing bills if they want to keep students' mailboxes. The company announced plans last week to retire Office 365 A1, the Student Use Benefit program, and free Exchange Online for Alumni. The changes generally take effect at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Office 365 A1 provides eligible institutions with web-based Office applications, Teams, and email at no charge. Its replacement, Microsoft 365 Education A0, excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also depends on paid faculty licensing and students actively using Windows devices for education. A spokesperson for the UK's Department for Education told The Register : "We are disappointed that Microsoft has made this decision. However, we are pleased to have successfully negotiated some additional concessions for the UK, giving schools, colleges and universities the time they need to be able to successfully transition to new licensing agreements." An industry insider said the loss of free Microsoft-hosted email could add thousands to institutions' bills. Another organization noted "significant concerns… around affordability, equitable treatment across the sector, and the longer-term implications of the changes." A spokesperson for UK education technology body Jisc told The Register that its "focus has been on ensuring that UK education providers are well supported and have sufficient time to assess their options." "We continue working closely with Microsoft and sector partners to support those discussions and help institutions make informed decisions about their future requirements." Also being retired are free Exchange Online for Alumni – which lets graduates retain their mailboxes – and the Student Use Benefit, providing student licenses at no additional charge when institutions purchase qualifying faculty licenses. Microsoft plans a paid alumni replacement. The Windows giant is also changing storage entitlements and introducing Microsoft 365 Education A7, its "most advanced education offering," which adds AI, security, governance, and device-management features. Asked why it was removing those services from the free tier, Microsoft framed the overhaul as a response to institutions' changing needs. A spokesperson told The Register : "Education institutions are evaluating AI, security, privacy, governance, and teaching and learning as connected priorities rather than separate technology decisions. "Microsoft is updating the portfolio now to provide a clearer path from foundational access to advanced capabilities, while enabling institutions to adopt technology according to their needs and readiness. This evolution reflects both the value Microsoft 365 Education has gained since the last pricing change nearly a decade ago and the structure of the new portfolio. "Microsoft's broader goal is not technology adoption for its

item.title: APOD: 2026 November 10 – Saturn Behind the Moon
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 10 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Saturn Behind the Moon Explanation: Sometimes Saturn disappears. It doesn’t really go away, of course — it just disappears from our view when Earth’s Moon moves in front. Such a Saturn ian eclipse, more formally called an occultation , was visible in early 2025 along a small swath of Earth — from Greenland through central Europe and into northern Africa . The featured image is a digital fusion of three images, the first of just Saturn before it disappeared, and then two more of the Moon with different exposure lengths. The images were taken from Sardinia , Italy , after sunset. The bright dot near Saturn is not a moon of Saturn , but rather the star 85 Aquarii , which is further behind Saturn than Saturn is behind the Moon. The next time the Moon moves in front of Saturn, as visible from some place on Earth , will be in 2031. item.title: Autumn Mornings Bring Valley Fog
item.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Autumn Mornings Bring Valley Fog Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search morning afternoon A natural-color satellite image from the morning shows white fog filling a branching network of river valleys, surrounded by brown and green terrain. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin A false-color satellite image from the afternoon shows the same area clear of fog, with rivers and lakes in dark blue winding through bright green vegetation. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin morning afternoon A natural-color satellite image from the morning shows white fog filling a branching network of river valleys, surrounded by brown and green terrain. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin A false-color satellite image from the afternoon shows the same area clear of fog, with rivers and lakes in dark blue winding through bright green vegetation. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin morning afternoon Curtain Toggle 2-Up Image Details On November 8, 2026, low clouds traced the branching valleys of the Appalachian Plateau and the Cumberland River in the morning (left, natural color) then burned off by afternoon (right, false color). The images were acquired with the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite and the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on NOAA-21 , respectively. NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin. On a cool November morning, low clouds traced the branching valleys of the Appalachian Plateau and the Cumberland River. By afternoon, they had faded, leaving clear skies over the autumn landscape. The change is visible in this pair of images from November 8, 2026. The MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite acquired the left image that morning. In this natural-color view, low clouds appear white as they fill many of the valleys. Autumn vegetation appears in shades of brown and green. The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on NOAA-21 acquired the right image that afternoon, after the clouds had dissipated and exposed the rivers and lakes beneath them. This false-color view makes it easier to distinguish water (dark blue) from vegetation (bright green). The clouds appear to be fog, a type of cloud that forms near the ground . Foggy mornings in the region are common this time of year. As nights lengthen, the ground has more time to radiate away the day’s heat, and the air just above it cools to the dew point —the temperature at which air becomes saturated and water vapor begins condensing into the tiny droplets that make up fog. item.title: Cisco to link all future products to its SaaS-y Cloud Control management tool
item.description: Cisco will no longer create products that don’t integrate with Cloud Control, its SaaS-y management platform that offers netadmins a single tool to manage all of the networking giant’s devices and much of its software portfolio. The networking giant announced Cloud Control in June 2025 and only made it available to customers in the USA. Cisco has previously told The Register that slow rollout reflects the fact that Cisco needs to nail privacy and other regulatory niceties, and deploy infrastructure, before introducing the service to other markets. It appears Cisco is now satisfied it has sorted out those issues. Jeff Schultz, Cisco’s senior vice president for portfolio strategy and marketing, today told the company’s Live conference in Australia that Cloud Control will come online in the European Union, UK, and Down Under in February 2027. Japan, India, and Canada will get their turn in May. Schultz said Cisco is “working tirelessly” to deploy Cloud Control across the world as soon as possible. He also revealed that, starting next year, Cisco will no longer ship products that don’t integrate with Cloud Control. That doesn’t mean those products will be manageable only if they can connect to Cloud Control. Instead, the decision reflects Cisco’s belief that the main thing stopping its customers buying more of its products is the complexity of operating them in concert. Schultz also feels that Cloud Control represents “platform advantage” for Cisco, because when users integrate networking, security, and observability the result is better manageability and resilience. Schultz also told the conference that Cisco will bundle its Thousand Eyes observability and security tool with the “Essentials” and “Advantage” licenses. “We admit it was hard to license and deploy,” he said during his keynote speech, adding that the tool will be deployed automatically with Wi‑Fi 6E and Wi‑Fi 7 hardware. Another product Cisco plans to bring to more customers is Live Protect, a tool that implements compensating controls for flaws that organizations can’t immediately patch. The product has become particularly useful since Anthropic's Mythos model, and similar AI offerings, made it possible to quickly find more software bugs and flaws and overwhelmed tech teams whose patching apparatus was not set up to handle hundreds of montly CVEs. Live Protect currently works on some of Cisco's datacenter switches, plus SD-WAN and WLAN controllers. From December, Cisco will extend it to 8000 series routers, secure firewalls, campus gateway, and to Cloud Control itself. From May 2027, Live Protect will work with Cisco’s ASR 9000 series service aggregation routers and Network Convergence System. "Expect this to be a major investment area," Schultz added. ®

item.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5056-5062: Charging Back Up!
item.description: Curiosity Navigation Curiosity Home Mission Overview Where is Curiosity? Mission Updates Science Overview Instruments Highlights Exploration Goals News and Features Multimedia Curiosity Raw Images Images Videos Audio Mosaics More Resources Mars Missions Mars Perseverance Rover Mars Curiosity Rover Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Mars Odyssey More Mars Missions Mars Home 3 min read Curiosity Blog, Sols 5056-5062: Charging Back Up! This image was taken by Right Navigation Camera onboard NASA’s Mars rover Curiosity on Sol 5062 (2026-11-02 05:40:15 UTC). NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS By Remington Free, Operations Systems Engineer, NASA-JPL Earth planning date: Friday, Oct. 30, 2026 Today’s plan covered 3 sols, 5060, 5061, and 5062, as we take a few recharging sols before getting back to our normal drilling activities. As you may know if you have been following the blog closely, we are in the middle of a drilling campaign on our target called “Nazca.” We’ve already drilled the hole, characterized the tailings from the drill hole with ChemCam, and have now done several sample dropoffs, both to our SAM and CheMin instruments within the belly of the rover. We still have a number of activities left to do as part of the campaign, including another dropoff to SAM for a different kind of analysis, and drilling cleanup activities. One of those activities is called “RAGE” (Rotate to Agitate for Granule Expulsion, a very fun acronym) where we essentially shake the drill to get any remaining sample out of it. We’ll also make sure to take lots of imaging to continue document the drill hole and tailings. In any case, those activities are very power-hungry for our rover! So today’s plan purposefully did not have a lot of activities in it so we could get a nice few power positive sols before we get back to drilling. Each of our three sols had a standard morning science block, with an extra exciting brand-new activity on 5061 (more on that shortly!). Over the three sols, we conducted remote science with ChemCam active and Remote Micro-Imager mosaics on some interesting targets (“Titicaca,” “Pampas,” and “Salta”), some Mastcam imaging of our calibration target and our drill target, several Navcam dust devil studies and Mastcam tau observations, and twilight imaging. Despite this plan being recharging/waiting, we got in lots of exciting science to continue to study the Nazca crystal formations and the nearby layered rocks and bedrock. On 5061, we also conducted a brand-new engineering activity to test parallelism over one of our downlink communications windows. As the rover gets older and our power output slowly decreases over the length of the mission, we are continuously looking for new ways to execute activities with less power use. One of our strategies is parallelism – having two activities execute at the same time will save power due to the rover being awake for less time. However, we need to vet pairs of activities ahead of time to ensure they are safe to run together. This

item.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5050-5055: It’s Nazca, Our 49th Drill Hole
item.description: Curiosity Navigation Curiosity Home Mission Overview Where is Curiosity? Mission Updates Science Overview Instruments Highlights Exploration Goals News and Features Multimedia Curiosity Raw Images Images Videos Audio Mosaics More Resources Mars Missions Mars Perseverance Rover Mars Curiosity Rover Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Mars Odyssey More Mars Missions Mars Home 3 min read Curiosity Blog, Sols 5050-5055: It’s Nazca, Our 49th Drill Hole This image of the Nazca drill hole was taken by Mast Camera (Mastcam) onboard NASA’s Mars rover Curiosity on Sol 5050 (2026-10-20 23:56:20 UTC). NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS Written by Susanne P. Schwenzer, Professor of Planetary Mineralogy at The Open University, UK Earth planning date: Friday, Oct. 23, 2026 As regular readers of this blog will know, we returned to the area where we found disc shaped inclusions in the rocks, which we interpreted as potential crystals. If they are indeed crystals, and we compare them to Earth, they could be very interesting indicators of the environmental conditions. Hence, the excitement in the team is high that we found a good block to drill. Good means first and foremost that it contains abundant potential crystals, but of course there is more before we drill. We passed the rover’s stability test, as all wheels have to be on solid ground before we extend the arm. Then we passed the preload test, which tests the stability of the rock and the forces the arm experiences when the drill bit presses into the rock. With all those tests passed, we successfully drilled our 49th drill hole, called “Nazca.” The drill campaign comes with many investigations before and after the drilling itself. Before the drill, we investigated the block with APXS, MAHLI and ChemCam – all on the target Nazca. After drilling, the sample was dropped off to CheMin, with the results still making their way from Mars to Earth. They are eagerly anticipated to reach us over the coming weekend. ChemCam obtained both passive spectral and active LIBS of the tailings and a LIBS measurement down the drill hole wall. Other ChemCam activities this week included a LIBS investigation of “Palpala,” which is a dark pebble. We are on the lookout for those pebbles for a while and find that not all of them have the same composition. To make sure we understand their origin, we are measuring them when there are some in reach that are big enough. If a pebble is too small, it can move when it is being hit by the laser. Hence, we need to look out for some that are big enough. Another such pebble was the target “Puna” identified in Friday’s planning. ChemCam LIBS on the target “Llama” is to get another depth profile to check whether our observations in the first such depth profile are consistently observed or whether they vary between locations. The target “Pacaya” is another measurement of the disc shaped forms that drew us back to this region. In addition to the LIBS measurements, ChemCam has several long distance RMIs in the plan. The

item.title: Global carbon emissions set to fall in 2026 due to Iran energy shock
item.description: The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz led to a spike in oil prices Anna Ivanova/Alamy Carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels are expected to drop this year for the first time in five years. The slowdown has been partly attributed to the energy shock triggered by the US and Israel’s war on Iran. The conflict, which began in February, led to a jump in oil prices after the Strait of Hormuz, the main trade route for about 20 per cent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas, was blockaded by Iran in response. This is still affecting petrol prices and household gas bills, and has seen countries around the world turn to alternative fuel types to boost energy security. Advertisement Read more Solar energy is going to power the world much sooner than you think Around 38.2 gigatonnes of CO2 are expected to be emitted in 2026 globally, according to the latest annual Global Carbon Budget – put together by more than 140 researchers. This is a 0.4 per cent decrease on the previous year, largely due to a projected 1.9 per cent fall in emissions from oil. The drop in oil use was partly offset by a 0.6 per cent increase in emissions from coal. Robbie Andrew at climate research group CICERO in Oslo, Norway, one of the report authors, says financial pressures due to the energy shock are likely to have caused the drop in emissions this year, which may turn out to be a “blip”. “On the assumption that there are no further crises, then you’d expect that emissions would bounce back,” says Andrew. The two biggest dips in emissions in the 21st century have been attributed to the covid-19 pandemic, which saw emissions drop by around 6 per cent in 2020, and the global financial crisis, which saw emissions drop around 2 per cent in 2009. The future outlook depends on how long the energy shock lasts, says Andrew, with governments forced to look at the economic case for continuing to subsidise fossil fuels. The rollout of renewable energy also played a part in bringing down carbon emissions. Electric vehicles and solar and wind power are predicted to offset 64 to 79 per cent of increasing emissions from demand growth through to 2028. Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter In China, the world’s biggest emitter of CO2, emissions are projected to decrease by 0.9 per cent in 2026 as the country continues to make strides with expanding renewable energy and electric vehicles. “What’s keeping emissions down is the renewable energy, and the price of oil actually suppresses this even more,” says Corinne Le Quéré at the University of East Anglia, UK, who also worked on the report. “So, that’s encouraging in a way, but it does mean that if the price of oil rebounds to pre-Iran [conflict] levels, most likely the emissions will rebound as well until we have enough further acceleration in renewable energy to really bring the emissions down durably.” Journal Reference: Nature Climate Change DOI: 10.1038/s41558-026-02821-8
